objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain the ELT, fire extinguisher, survival, signaling, overwater, ballistic parachute and Emergency Autoland rules and limits that apply to the airplane and the kind of flight you are flying, pick the gear for 48 to 72 hours on your own, and give passengers a clear, professional briefing on all of it.
why: As a commercial pilot you carry people who trust you to have thought about the worst day, and some rules only switch on when you fly for hire [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(12)]]. Rescue can take days: an injured survivor's life expectancy can fall as much as 80 percent in the first 24 hours [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]].

prereading.label: 14 CFR 91.207

prereading.label: AIM 6-2-4

warmup: Think first: you fly two paying passengers across a lake that is too wide to glide across. Your airplane has a working ELT and a fire extinguisher. What else does the law say must be on board for this flight, and what would you add even though no rule asks for it?

key_terms.def: A battery-powered transmitter that helps searchers find a downed aircraft. It works on 121.5, 243.0 or 406 MHz [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]].
A digital ELT that can carry owner and position data, is detected by satellite, and includes a low-power 121.5 MHz homing signal [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]].
The satellite distress alerting system. It stopped listening on 121.5 and 243.0 MHz in 2009 [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]].
Part 135 operations need an automatic type ELT; most other operations may use an approved personal or automatic type [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(a)]].
A flare-type signal. At least one is required when flying for hire over water beyond power-off gliding distance from shore [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(12)]].
Land next to the water above the high water mark, not land that is sometimes under water [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(12)]].
For airplanes, flight over water more than 50 NM horizontally from the nearest shoreline [[60:6|14 CFR 1.1]].
A forced or precautionary landing on water [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].
The swell system with the greatest height from trough to crest [[34:49|AIM 6-3-3]].
The side of a swell toward the observer. The back side is the side away from the observer [[34:49|AIM 6-3-3]].
A system that rockets a parachute out so it lowers the whole airplane slowly to the ground [[24:345|AFH 17-11]].
A system that can take control if the pilot is incapacitated, pick an airport, fly there and land [[34:340|AIM PCG E-1]].

chunks.title: What this task asks of a commercial pilot

body.p: This task is about the gear that keeps people alive after something goes wrong: the ELT, the fire extinguisher, survival gear for heat, cold, mountains and water, and, if the airplane has them, a ballistic parachute and an Emergency Autoland system (ACS CA.IX.D.K1 to K5).

The element list in the commercial ACS is word for word the same as the private one (ACS PA.IX.D and CA.IX.D). What changes is you. A commercial pilot flies for hire, and some equipment rules only apply then. A good example: flying for hire over water beyond power-off gliding distance from shore needs approved flotation gear for each occupant and at least one pyrotechnic signaling device [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(12)]].

Many commercial pilots go on to fly under Part 135, which brings more: an automatic type ELT [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(a)]], hand fire extinguishers in set places [[6:58|14 CFR 135.155]], liferafts for extended overwater flights [[6:65|14 CFR 135.167]] and a required passenger briefing with printed cards [[6:36|14 CFR 135.117]]. This lesson shows those contrasts where the regulation states them.

callout.text: Part 23 design standard: safety and survival equipment required by the operating rules must be reliable, readily accessible, easy to identify and clearly marked with how it works [[60:118|14 CFR 23.2535]].

ACS Appendix 3: if the airplane has a ballistic parachute, follow the manufacturer's arming and disarming steps before and after flight. The examiner may test it by simulation and briefing, never by real deployment.

check.q: Which part of this task changes when you fly for hire over water beyond gliding distance from shore?
check.a: You must carry approved flotation gear readily available to each occupant and at least one pyrotechnic signaling device [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(12)]].

chunks.title: The ELT: what it does and where it falls short

body.p: ELTs are required in most general aviation airplanes. They transmit on 121.5 MHz, 243.0 MHz or 406 MHz. The 121.5 and 243.0 units are analog. The 406 MHz unit is digital, can be coded with the owner's contact data, and newer models can send the aircraft's position too [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]].

head: 121.5 / 243.0 MHz (analog)
406 MHz (digital)
rows: Satellite detection
None since 2009; depends on ATC or an overflying aircraft hearing it [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]]
Detected by Cospas-Sarsat; owner data goes to a Rescue Coordination Center [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]]
How fast SAR responds
Often waits for an overdue report; can take hours [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]]
Response can start in minutes [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]]
Search area
Wider
Narrower search area; 121.5 MHz homing for the final search [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]]
Registration
No owner database to check
Must be registered with NOAA [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]]

body.p: An armed ELT is built to switch on by itself from crash forces and transmit for at least 48 hours over a wide temperature range. But it only helps if it survives the crash and actually activates [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]]. That is the big limit: it may not work. So you and your passengers should know how to turn it on by hand and how to check that it is transmitting [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]].

Flying an airplane with only a 121.5 MHz ELT? The FAA and NOAA encourage owners to switch to 406 MHz, and pilots who do not own the airplane are told to check the ELT and, as appropriate, carry a 406 MHz personal locator beacon [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

callout.text: When a crash landing or ditching is coming, actuate the ELT if the installation permits, and include its status in your distress call [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]]. Do not count on the crash switch alone.
121.5 waits for someone to listen. 406 calls the satellite.

check.q: Why might rescuers start much later for a 121.5 MHz ELT than for a 406 MHz one?
check.a: Satellites no longer monitor 121.5 MHz, there is no owner database to check false alerts, so SAR usually waits for confirmation such as an overdue report, which can take hours [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]] [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

body.p: The rule is 14 CFR 91.207. Part 135 operations (and certain Part 121 and 125 operations) need an approved automatic type ELT. Other operations may use an approved personal type or automatic type. Either way it must be in operable condition [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(a)]].

bullets: Mounting: attached so crash damage is unlikely. Fixed and deployable automatic types go as far aft as practicable [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(b)]].

Battery: replace (or recharge) after more than 1 cumulative hour of use, or when 50 percent of its useful life, as set by the transmitter maker, has expired. Mark the new date on the outside of the transmitter and in the maintenance record. The 50 percent rule does not apply to batteries, such as water-activated ones, that storage barely affects [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]].
Inspection: within 12 calendar months of the last one, for installation, battery corrosion, the controls and crash sensor, and a sufficient radiated signal [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]].
The PHAK repeats these items [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]]. Application: check the ELT dates in the records and on the transmitter as part of your preflight.

body.p: 91.207(e) and (f) list several exceptions. These four matter most to a pilot of a small single:

head: Exception in 91.207
What it allows
rows: Ferry (e)
Ferry a newly bought airplane to where the ELT will be installed, or an airplane with an inoperative ELT to a repair place; only required crew aboard [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(e)]]
Local training (f)(3)
Training flights that stay entirely within 50 NM of the airport where they began [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)]]
One-seat airplane (f)(9)
Aircraft equipped to carry not more than one person [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)]]
ELT removed (f)(10)
Up to 90 days, with a record entry and an 'ELT not installed' placard in view of the pilot [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)]]

body.p: Testing: test the ELT the way the manufacturer says, ideally in a shielded room or test container. If that is not possible, an analog unit may be tested only in the first 5 minutes after any hour, for no more than three audible sweeps (or coordinate with the nearest tower). A 406 MHz unit is tested only per the manufacturer's instructions. Airborne tests are not authorized [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

False alarms look exactly like real ones and waste searches. Listen on 121.5 MHz before engine shutdown at the end of every flight. If you hear a signal, turn off your ELT to see if it is yours, and if it was, tell the nearest air traffic facility [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]]. In flight, if you hear an ELT, report where you first heard it, last heard it, and where it was strongest, with your altitude and the frequency [[34:32|AIM 6-2-4]].

callout.text: The 50 NM training exception covers only training that stays entirely within 50 NM of the departure airport [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)]]. A for-hire flight or a long cross-country needs a working ELT.

check.q: A new ELT battery's useful life, set by the manufacturer, is 6 years counted from 2024. Under 91.207, ignoring use time, in what year is it due?
check.a: When 50 percent of its useful life has expired: half of 6 years is 3 years, 2024 + 3 = 2027 [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]].

chunks.title: Fire extinguishers and fire on board

body.p: A fire in flight needs immediate, decisive action, and the AFM/POH procedure for your airplane comes first [[24:358|AFH 18-9]]. The extinguisher is only part of the answer: in the AFH it appears only in the cabin fire procedure [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

head: Fire type
First clue
Generic actions (POH first)
rows: Engine
Smoke or flames from the cowling, or the cowling skin bubbling or melting [[24:358|AFH 18-9]]
Mixture idle cutoff and fuel selector off, ignition left on to burn off fuel; do not restart if it goes out [[24:358|AFH 18-9]]
Electrical
Smell of burning insulation [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]
Find and isolate the circuit; if you cannot, turn off battery master and alternator if flight conditions allow [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]
Cabin
Smoke from careless smoking, electrical or heater faults [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]
Shut down the faulty system, use the extinguisher, then ventilate; land as soon as possible [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]

body.p: Extinguisher limits you must know: open the cabin vents only after the extinguisher (if available) is used. If smoke gets worse when the vents open, close them at once: the airflow may be feeding the fire or the fire may be in the heater or nose baggage area [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]. And removing power from an electrical fire does not stop material that is already burning [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

Application: a hand extinguisher cannot reach an engine compartment fire from the cabin. That fire can rekindle with changes in airflow or airspeed and can keep burning out of view, so in a single-engine airplane plan a forced landing and treat the airplane as expendable [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

Part 135 contrast: a passenger-carrying Part 135 aircraft needs approved hand extinguishers whose agent type and quantity suit the fires likely to occur, [[6:58|14 CFR 135.155]], with at least one on the flight deck [[6:59|14 CFR 135.155(b)]], plus one in the passenger compartment when there are 10 to 30 passenger seats [[6:59|14 CFR 135.155(c)]]. Crews train on which type of extinguisher to use on different classes of fire [[6:108|14 CFR 135.331]].

callout.text: Brief the extinguisher's location and how it works on every flight: it is the F in the SAFETY briefing [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]]. Know your own unit's label before you need it.

check.q: You use the extinguisher on a cabin fire, then open the vents and the smoke thickens. What now?
check.a: Close the vents at once; more airflow may be feeding the fire, or the fire may be in the heating system or nose baggage area [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

body.p: The ACS asks you to manage the risk of survival gear (water, clothing, shelter) for 48 to 72 hours (ACS CA.IX.D.R1). The sources explain why that window matters.

bullets: An injured survivor's life expectancy can drop as much as 80 percent in the first 24 hours, and uninjured survivors' chances fall quickly after the first 3 days [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]].
Without a flight plan, an Air Force review found 36 hours normally pass before family concern starts an alert [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]].
On a VFR flight plan, a search starts if you have not responded within half an hour after your ETA at the final destination [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]].
A working ELT transmits for at least 48 hours [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]].

body.p: So the plan has two halves. First, shorten the wait: file a flight plan, tell someone your route, file only to your first landing and refile each leg, stay on course, and close the plan as soon as you arrive [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]]. Second, carry what you need to last until they come: for flight over uninhabited land, take and know how to use survival equipment for the climate and terrain [[34:35|AIM 6-2-6]].

After a crash landing, stay with the airplane unless you have good reason to think you will not be found, and get your signals ready [[34:47|AIM 6-3-2]]. The airplane is bigger and easier to see than you.

callout.text: A long flight plan with several stops and one ETA to the final destination can mean nobody looks for you until 30 minutes after that final ETA, even if you went down on the first leg [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]].

check.q: Why does the AIM say to file only to your first intended landing and refile for each leg?
check.a: With one long plan, a mishap on an early leg may not trigger a search until 30 minutes after the ETA at the final destination [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]].

body.p: Before a trip over remote areas, ask whether you have the right clothing, water and survival gear on board in case of a forced landing [[1:48|PHAK 2-9]].

Heat: plan around water. Dehydration comes from hot flight decks, wind, humidity and diuretic drinks like coffee, tea, alcohol and caffeinated sodas. Signs include headache, fatigue, cramps, sleepiness and dizziness [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]].

bullets: The PHAK guide is two to four quarts of water every 24 hours, per person [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]].
Most people only feel thirsty after a 1.5 quart deficit, about 2 percent of body weight, and a sip turns the thirst off too early [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]].
Carry a container so you can measure what you drink, and do not wait for thirst [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]].
Heatstroke may start with dehydration symptoms, or show up only as a collapse [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]].

body.p: Hot weather also cuts performance. High density altitude means longer takeoff and landing runs and a lower climb rate [[34:163|AIM 7-6-7]]. A hot, heavy takeoff that goes wrong is a quick way to need your survival kit.

Cold: a landing in snow should be flown like a ditching, in the same configuration, watching for whiteout and loss of depth perception on wide open terrain [[24:356|AFH 18-7]]. In snow you can make ground signals by dragging, shoveling or tramping; the depressions look black from the air [[34:36|AIM FIG 6-2-1]]. Some regions go further: in its seaplane safety paragraph, the AIM notes that survival kits are required by law for flight into sparsely settled areas of Canada and Alaska, and recommends summer and winter kits kept in one easy-to-reach container [[34:165|AIM 7-6-9]] [[34:166|AIM 7-6-9]].

callout.text: Application: dress for the ground you are flying over, not for the heated cabin. The sources give no cold-weather clothing list, so build one with your CFI for your season and route.

check.q: Three people may wait 72 hours in the desert. Using the low end of the PHAK guide, how much water should you carry?
check.a: 2 quarts x 3 people x 3 days = 18 quarts at the low end; the high end of the guide doubles it to 36 [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]].

chunks.title: Mountains, forests and the controlled crash

body.p: In the mountains, flat fields for forced landings are almost nonexistent and winds and clouds change fast [[34:162|AIM 7-6-7]]. The AIM's first advice: file a flight plan, route over populated areas and well-known passes, and keep enough altitude to glide to a safe landing if the engine quits [[34:162|AIM 7-6-7]]. Always fly with an escape route in mind [[34:163|AIM 7-6-7]].

If you still end up going down in rough terrain, survival depends on two things: keeping the cabin intact by letting the wings, gear and fuselage bottom absorb the stop, and keeping each body from hitting the inside of the cabin, which comes down to seat and harness security [[24:351|AFH 18-2]].

Groundspeed matters most. Doubling it quadruples the destructive energy, so touch down at the lowest controllable airspeed [[24:352|AFH 18-3]]. A typical light airplane protects occupants up to 9 G forward. At a steady 9 G, 50 mph needs about 9.4 ft to stop and 100 mph about 37.6 ft [[24:352|AFH 18-3]].

bullets: Trees: normal landing configuration, head into the wind, and touch at minimum airspeed (not below stall) in a nose-high attitude so the wings and belly cushion the contact [[24:355|AFH 18-6]].
Low, closely spaced trees with dense crowns beat tall, thin ones. A 75 ft free fall hits at about 40 knots, roughly 4,000 fpm [[24:355|AFH 18-6]].
Aim for even contact on both wings, and keep the fuselage away from heavy trunks [[24:355|AFH 18-6]].
Dense crops and brush absorb energy well [[24:351|AFH 18-2]].

callout.text: Do not change your mind more than once when picking a spot. A well-flown crash landing in poor terrain can be safer than an uncontrolled touchdown on a good field [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

check.q: Why does the AFH want low, dense trees rather than tall ones with thin tops?
check.a: Tall, thin tops leave too much free-fall height; 75 ft of free fall means about 40 knots, roughly 4,000 fpm, at impact [[24:355|AFH 18-6]].

body.p: Overwater, your chances depend on how well the crew knows the emergency procedures and on having water survival equipment that works [[34:35|AIM 6-2-6]]. The rules that apply grow with the kind of flight.

head: Flight
Required equipment
rows: Part 91, not for hire
No flotation rule, because 91.205(b)(12) applies only for hire; the decision is yours [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(12)]]
Part 91, for hire, beyond power-off gliding distance from shore
Approved flotation gear readily available to each occupant, and at least one pyrotechnic signaling device [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(12)]]
Part 135, extended overwater (more than 50 NM from shore)

Life preserver with a survivor locator light for each occupant, enough liferafts, each raft equipped with listed survival gear, and a survival type ELT attached to a raft [[6:65|14 CFR 135.167]] [[6:66|14 CFR 135.167(c)]] [[60:6|14 CFR 1.1]]

body.p: Each Part 135 raft carries at least a survivor locator light and a pyrotechnic signal, plus either a survival kit for the route or a long list that includes a signaling mirror, whistle, dye marker, flashlight, a 2-day food supply of at least 1,000 calories per day per person, and water or a desalting kit [[6:65|14 CFR 135.167]] [[6:66|14 CFR 135.167]]. That list is a good model for what a for-hire Part 91 pilot might choose to carry.

Which flotation gear? FAA-approved life vests (TSO-C13E) are inflatable. Bulky Coast Guard type foam PFDs can block the narrow exits of small aircraft. The wearer inflates the vest after getting out of the aircraft, using CO2 cartridges with an oral tube as backup, and the vest has a water-activated light [[34:166|AIM 7-6-9]].

callout.text: Inflate a life vest only after you are out of the airplane [[34:166|AIM 7-6-9]]. An inflated vest in a sinking cabin can trap you against the ceiling.
Can't glide to shore and paid to fly? Float for each and a flare.

check.a: Land next to the water above the high water mark, not counting land that is sometimes under water [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(12)]].

chunks.title: Ditching: read the sea, pick the heading

body.p: A good ditching usually means less violent deceleration than a bad tree landing. An airplane ditched at minimum speed in a normal landing attitude does not sink right away: intact wings and fuel tanks can float it for several minutes [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].

Before you touch the water: declare (MAYDAY, or squawk 7700 if you are not talking to anyone), give the ELT status, aircraft color, people on board and emergency equipment, actuate the ELT, and try to ditch near a surface vessel [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]]. If the coast is out of reach, ditch before the fuel runs out so you still have power [[34:51|AIM 6-3-3]].

Success depends, in order, on the sea and wind, the type of aircraft, and pilot skill [[34:49|AIM 6-3-3]]. The one rule: avoid the face of a swell. Land parallel to the swell, preferably on top or on the back side, and of the two parallel headings take the one with more headwind [[34:50|AIM 6-3-3]].

bullets: Two swell systems at right angles: land parallel to the primary one and down the secondary one; if they are equal, try a heading 45 degrees down swell to both [[34:50|AIM 6-3-3]].
A big swell: in a landplane, accept more crosswind rather than land into the swell [[34:50|AIM 6-3-3]].
Wind: read the long wind streaks on the water; whitecaps fall forward with the wind [[34:50|AIM 6-3-3]].
Pick a spot with fewer shadows and whitecaps; only about 500 ft is needed [[34:50|AIM 6-3-3]].

body.p: Touchdown: fly low over the water, slow to about ten knots above stall with power, and touch at the lowest safe speed and sink rate, nose up [[34:50|AIM 6-3-3]] [[34:51|AIM 6-3-3]]. Over glassy water or at night it is easy to misjudge height by 50 ft or more, so hold 9 to 12 degrees nose up with 10 to 20 percent above stall speed until you touch [[34:51|AIM 6-3-3]]. The AFH adds: use no more than intermediate flaps in a low-wing airplane and keep a retractable gear up unless the POH says otherwise [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].

check.q: You can land parallel to the primary swell on two opposite headings. How do you choose?
check.a: Pick the one with the most headwind component [[34:50|AIM 6-3-3]].

body.p: Signals start in the air. A distress call should begin with MAYDAY, preferably said three times, and it commands radio silence on that frequency. If your station does not answer, 121.5 MHz is the emergency frequency, guarded by most towers, radar facilities and direction finding stations [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]]. Climbing, if possible, improves radio and radar contact [[34:45|AIM 6-3-2]].

On the ground, use the ground-air visual code. Lay out symbols at least 10 ft high with as much color contrast as possible, and also use radio, flares, smoke or anything else that draws attention. A pilot overhead acknowledges by rocking the wings [[34:36|AIM FIG 6-2-1]]. Body signals work too: stand in the open, against a plain background, and repeat each signal slowly until the pilot understands [[34:35|AIM 6-2-6]].

A yellow cross on a crash site means it has already been reported [[34:35|AIM 6-2-6]]. If you find a downed aircraft, fix its position as accurately as possible, report it, and orbit to guide others if you can [[34:35|AIM 6-2-6]].

First aid: the sources say little for small airplanes. Part 135 contrast: a first-aid kit with a listed content (bandages, antiseptic swabs, splints, gloves and more) is required only for aircraft with more than 19 passenger seats [[6:72|14 CFR 135.177]] [[6:73|14 CFR 135.177]], so it never applies to a small single. The PHAK does give first aid for fuel, oil and hydraulic fluid exposure, for example flushing fuel from the eyes with clean water for at least 15 minutes [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]].

callout.text: Application: carry signals you can use with injured hands: a whistle, a mirror and a light, all listed for Part 135 rafts [[6:66|14 CFR 135.167]]. Brief where they are.

check.q: You are down in a snowfield with no fabric or wood. How can you make the 'require assistance' symbol?
check.a: Tramp, drag or shovel a V in the snow at least 10 ft high; the depressions look black from the air [[34:36|AIM FIG 6-2-1]].

body.p: A ballistic parachute rockets a canopy out so it lowers the whole airplane slowly. Deployed within an acceptable flight regime, occupants usually survive the touchdown with minor or no injuries, but the airframe is lost [[24:345|AFH 17-11]] [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

When to deploy: the AFH gives examples such as a catastrophic loss of controllability from a collision or mechanical failure, an actual loss of control, or pilot incapacitation [[24:371|AFH 18-22]]. Deploy only within an acceptable flight regime; the exact limits come from the manufacturer, so study their guidance and follow it [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

bullets: Preflight: check the mounts, the safety pin and flag, and the activation handle and cable [[24:345|AFH 17-11]].
Arm and disarm the system exactly as the manufacturer says, before and after flight [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].
Brief any passenger who can reach the handle on when a deployment is safe and the basic steps. Normally a passenger would deploy only if the pilot were incapacitated [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].
After landing, a deployed canopy plus surface wind is a hazard; everyone should know how to evacuate [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

body.p: The risk (ACS CA.IX.D.R2) cuts both ways. The AFH's own lesson from forced landings is that the desire to save the airplane leads pilots to bad choices, and a pilot should sometimes sacrifice the airplane so the occupants walk away [[24:351|AFH 18-2]]. Application: waiting too long to pull because the airplane is expensive is the same trap; the other risks are a pin left in or a passenger who pulls at the wrong time.

callout.text: On the checkride you simulate and brief the deployment. Actual deployment is never part of the test (ACS Appendix 3).

check.q: Who should you brief on deployment conditions and steps, and when would they use it?
check.a: Any passenger with access to the deployment mechanism; generally they would deploy only if the pilot were incapacitated [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

chunks.title: Emergency Autoland: what it does and does not do

body.p: If a pilot is incapacitated, an Emergency Autoland system may take over and deviate to meet the emergency [[34:28|AIM 6-1-1]]. If it senses erratic flying it stabilizes the airplane and checks whether the pilot responds. With no response it starts an emergency descent, then an automated landing. A pilot or a passenger can also activate it by hand [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

bullets: It broadcasts on the last selected frequency and on 121.5 MHz in a synthetic voice and squawks 7700, then pauses 25 seconds so ATC can move traffic [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].
Within 12 miles of the runway and at or below 12,000 ft MSL it talks on the tower frequency or CTAF and keeps reporting by ADS-B, with a one-minute-out call [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].
It chooses an airport by weather, wind, runway length and towered status, only among airports with an RNAV or GPS approach [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].
If it loses GPS it flies straight ahead and does not try to land until GPS returns [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

callout.text: Today's EAL does not see or avoid other aircraft, take ATC instructions or NOTAMs, avoid MOAs, restricted areas or TFRs, or turn on the lights [[24:372|AFH 18-23]]. Controllers are told to assume it will not acknowledge them [[34:340|AIM PCG E-1]].

body.p: Application: brief passengers to activate it if you are unresponsive or clearly unable to fly, show them the control, and tell them to stay belted and let it fly. The manufacturer's guide gives the exact steps.

check.q: An EAL system loses GPS during its diversion. What does it do?
check.a: It keeps flying straight ahead without trying to land until GPS coverage returns [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

body.p: Before takeoff the PIC must make sure each person is briefed on how to fasten and unfasten the seat belt and shoulder harness [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)]]. The PHAK SAFETY list covers the rest, including the fire extinguisher and the emergency/survival kit [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].

head: SAFETY item
Emergency gear to add for this task
rows: S: seat belts, harness, seat locked [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]]
Brace position and belts tight for a forced landing
A: air vents, environment, discomfort [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]]
Where the cabin vents are, in case of smoke
F: fire extinguisher location and operation [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]]
Where it is, how your unit works (read its label), who uses it
E: exits, evacuation, survival kit [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]]
ELT switch, life vests (inflate outside), parachute handle, EAL control
T: traffic, sterile flight deck [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]]
When not to talk to you
Y: your questions [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]]
Check they understood the deploy and activate conditions

body.p: Part 135 contrast: the Part 135 oral briefing must cover, among other items, the location of survival equipment, ditching and flotation use on extended overwater flights, and the location and operation of fire extinguishers, backed by printed cards placed where each passenger can use them [[6:35|14 CFR 135.117]] [[6:36|14 CFR 135.117]]. Using that list on a for-hire Part 91 flight is a good professional habit.
For S3, simulate the parachute deployment: point to the handle, say the conditions, then the manufacturer's steps, without pulling (ACS Appendix 3).

check.q: What one briefing item does 91.107 require for every passenger before takeoff?
check.a: How to fasten and unfasten their safety belt and, if installed, shoulder harness [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)]].

head: Error
Fix
rows: Not knowing the ELT inspection or battery dates
Check the logbook and the date on the transmitter during preflight [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]] [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]]
Assuming the 50 NM training exception covers a trip
It covers only training entirely within 50 NM of the departure airport [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)]]
Opening vents before using the extinguisher
Extinguisher first, then ventilate; close the vents if smoke grows [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]
Survival gear buried in the baggage area
Keep the kit in one container that is easy to reach, preferably one that floats [[34:166|AIM 7-6-9]]
Briefing to inflate vests in the cabin
Inflate after exiting [[34:166|AIM 7-6-9]]
Leaving the wreck to walk out
Stay with the airplane unless you have good reason to believe you won't be found [[34:47|AIM 6-3-2]]
Skipping the parachute pin and flag on preflight
Check mounts, pin and flag, handle and cable [[24:345|AFH 17-11]]

check.q: Your passenger asks if she should inflate her vest as soon as you say 'ditching'. What do you tell her?
check.a: No. Put it on, but inflate it only after getting out of the airplane [[34:166|AIM 7-6-9]].

f1.caption: Figure 18-2. Stopping distance vs. groundspeed. (AFH 18-3)
f1.alt: Two airplanes beside a ruler marked in feet under a 9G deceleration label. At 50 mph the airplane stops in 9.4 feet; at 100 mph the gouge in the ground is 37.6 feet long.

f2.caption: Figure 18-4. Tree landing. (AFH 18-6)
f2.alt: A high-wing airplane rests nose-high in the crowns of a dense stand of trees, both wings spread across the branches, with tree trunks, a lost wheel and debris on the grass below.

f3.caption: FIG 6-2-1. Ground-Air Visual Code for Use by Survivors. (AIM 6-2-6, page 6-2-8)
f3.alt: A table of five survivor symbols: V require assistance, X require medical assistance, N no, Y yes, an arrow for proceeding in this direction, and SOS if in doubt, with six layout instructions below.

f4.caption: FIG 6-3-4. (50 knot wind) (AIM 6-3-3, page 6-3-4)
f4.alt: Swell lines with a wind arrow at an angle. A small airplane lands straight into the wind; a larger one lands on a compromise heading between wind and swell. Notes: low landing speeds land into the wind, high landing speeds choose a compromise, both land on the back side of the swell.

f5.caption: FIG 6-3-5. Wind-Swell-Ditch Heading. (AIM 6-3-3, page 6-3-5)
f5.alt: Top: airplanes landing parallel to the major swell, rated best on the crest, good in the trough and on the left slope, fair on the right slope. Bottom: landing across the swell, good on the back side, poor on the face.

f6.caption: Figure 17-13. A ballistic recovery parachute is a popular safety feature available on some LSA. (AFH 17-11)
f6.alt: Aerial photo of a low-wing airplane hanging under a large blue parachute with a red center, descending over desert.

scenario.title: The company trip over the mountains in November
scenario.setup: You fly your employer's four-seat piston single, which has a 121.5 MHz ELT, a ballistic parachute and an Emergency Autoland system. Tomorrow you take two employees on a 3-hour Part 91 trip across a mountain range with snow above 6,000 ft. The forecast is good, but the route crosses forest with few roads. The logbook shows the last ELT inspection 11 months ago.

questions.q: Is the ELT legal for this trip, and what limit should worry you anyway?
questions.a: Yes if it is operable, the battery date is good and it was inspected within 12 calendar months [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]]. But satellites stopped monitoring 121.5 MHz in 2009, so someone must hear it; consider carrying a 406 MHz personal locator beacon [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]] [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

questions.q: How do you plan the route?
questions.a: File a flight plan and route over populated areas and well-known passes, high enough to glide to a safe landing, with an escape route in mind [[34:162|AIM 7-6-7]] [[34:163|AIM 7-6-7]].

questions.q: What survival gear do you pack for three people for 72 hours?
questions.a: Survival equipment for the climate and terrain [[34:35|AIM 6-2-6]], clothing for snow, shelter, signaling gear, and at least 18 quarts of water (2 quarts x 3 people x 3 days) [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]]. Keep the kit in one container that is easy to reach [[34:166|AIM 7-6-9]].

questions.q: What do you add to the passenger briefing for this airplane?
questions.a: SAFETY items including the extinguisher and survival kit [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]], plus who may pull the parachute handle (only if you are incapacitated), the basic steps, and how to evacuate under a canopy in wind [[24:371|AFH 18-22]]; and how and when to activate EAL [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

questions.q: Over the forest, the engine fails at 8,500 ft MSL, 4,000 ft above the trees, with no field in sight. How does the parachute fit your decision?
questions.a: A forced landing in dense trees is survivable if done nose-high at minimum speed [[24:355|AFH 18-6]], but no suitable field and a parachute on board make deployment a strong option; follow the manufacturer's limits for speed and altitude [[24:371|AFH 18-22]]. Do not let the wish to save the airplane delay the choice [[24:351|AFH 18-2]].

questions.q: You land safely under the canopy in a clearing, uninjured. What next?
questions.a: Get clear watching for the canopy in the wind [[24:371|AFH 18-22]], stay with the airplane and prepare signals [[34:47|AIM 6-3-2]], such as a large V tramped in the snow [[34:36|AIM FIG 6-2-1]]. Your flight plan starts a search 30 minutes after your ETA [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]].

skills.do: Point out the ELT, extinguisher, survival kit and any parachute or EAL controls, and explain which equipment this flight needs by rule and which you chose for the terrain, climate and water. The ACS gives no numeric tolerance.
skills.practice: Before each flight, say the ELT inspection and battery dates from the records [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]] and name one item you carry for the route's terrain or climate [[34:35|AIM 6-2-6]].

skills.do: Give a clear briefing on the use of every piece of emergency equipment and survival gear on board, in plain words, as if to a real passenger.
skills.practice: Give the SAFETY briefing on every flight [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]], adding vests (inflate outside) on overwater flights [[34:166|AIM 7-6-9]].

skills.do: If the airplane has a ballistic parachute, show the arming and disarming steps and simulate the deployment sequence without pulling the handle (ACS Appendix 3).
skills.practice: Rehearse with your CFI: name a trigger (collision, loss of control, incapacitation), point to the handle and recite the manufacturer's steps [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

quiz.q: Since 2009, what has the Cospas-Sarsat satellite system listened for?
options: 121.5 MHz only
406 MHz alerts, not 121.5 or 243.0 MHz
243.0 MHz only
All three ELT frequencies
quiz.why: Cospas-Sarsat stopped monitoring 121.5 and 243.0 MHz in 2009; it detects 406 MHz beacons [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]].

quiz.q: After replacing an ELT battery, where must the new expiration date go?
options: On the outside of the transmitter and in the aircraft maintenance record
Only in the pilot's logbook, kept on board with the airworthiness certificate
On a placard on the panel beside the ELT remote switch, in view of the pilot
On the airworthiness certificate, as endorsed by the mechanic who did the work
quiz.why: The new date must be legibly marked on the outside of the transmitter and entered in the maintenance record [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]].

quiz.q: You must test an analog 121.5 MHz ELT in the airplane, not in a shielded room. When may you do it?
options: Any time you are on the ground, as long as the test lasts under 1 minute
Only in flight at altitude, to check the range of the signal on 121.5
Only in the first 5 minutes after any hour, no more than three sweeps
Only between 0000 and 0500 local, when 121.5 MHz traffic is lightest
quiz.why: Analog units should be tested only in the first 5 minutes after the hour, for no more than three audible sweeps, unless coordinated with the tower; airborne tests are not authorized [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

quiz.q: Unless the POH says otherwise, what is the first step for an engine compartment fire in flight?
options: Master switch off, then radios off to cut all electrical sources
Dive steeply to blow the fire out, keeping the engine running for power
Open the cabin vents and the storm window to clear the smoke first
Mixture idle cutoff and fuel selector off, ignition left on
quiz.why: Shut off fuel with mixture idle cutoff and the fuel selector off, leaving the ignition on to use up fuel in the lines [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].

quiz.q: When should you open the cabin vents during a cabin fire?
options: Immediately, before anything else, to clear smoke from the cockpit
Only after landing, because open vents feed the fire in flight
Never in flight, because moving air always makes a cabin fire worse
Only after the fire extinguisher (if available) is used
quiz.why: Smoke may be removed by opening the vents, but only after the extinguisher is used; close them if the smoke increases [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

quiz.q: According to the PHAK, why is thirst a poor guide to how much water you need?
options: Thirst starts only after a 1.5 quart deficit and a small sip turns it off
Thirst is always triggered by caffeine, so it reflects drinks rather than need
Thirst starts too early and makes you drink more water than your body needs
Thirst does not occur at altitude or in cold weather, so it cannot be a guide
quiz.why: Most people become thirsty at a 1.5 quart deficit (2 percent of body weight); the mechanism arrives too late and is turned off too easily [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]].

quiz.q: Forced to land in a forest, which trees does the AFH prefer?
options: Tall trees with thin tops
A single large tree to stop quickly
Low, closely spaced trees with wide, dense crowns
Widely spaced trees to fly between while airborne
quiz.why: Low, closely spaced trees with dense crowns close to the ground are much better; tall thin tops allow too much free fall [[24:355|AFH 18-6]].

quiz.q: For an airplane, an extended over-water operation is flight over water more than how far from the nearest shoreline?
options: Power-off gliding distance
50 NM
25 NM
100 NM
quiz.why: For aircraft other than helicopters it means more than 50 NM horizontally from the nearest shoreline [[60:6|14 CFR 1.1]].

quiz.q: In the AIM, which factor matters most for a successful ditching?
options: Pilot skill and technique
Sea conditions and wind
Type of aircraft
Time of day
quiz.why: In order of importance: sea conditions and wind, type of aircraft, then skill and technique of the pilot [[34:49|AIM 6-3-3]].

quiz.q: Which of these can today's Emergency Autoland systems NOT do?
options: Squawk 7700
Broadcast on 121.5 MHz
Avoid other aircraft and TFRs
Select an airport using weather and runway length
quiz.why: EAL does not detect and avoid other aircraft or avoid TFRs and other special airspace [[24:372|AFH 18-23]]; it does squawk 7700, broadcast on 121.5 and choose an airport [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

final_quiz.q: Just before shutdown you hear an ELT tone on 121.5 MHz after a firm landing. What do you do?
options: Shut down and leave, since a tone on 121.5 MHz after landing is always someone else's ELT
Remove the ELT battery and continue the flight, since it is only a false alarm from the landing
Call the Rescue Coordination Center to cancel any search and leave the ELT on until they confirm
Turn off your ELT; if the signal stops it was yours, so notify the nearest air traffic facility
final_quiz.why: Turn off your ELT to check if it is transmitting; if it was activated, maintenance may be needed and you should contact the nearest air traffic facility [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

final_quiz.q: Your ELT was removed for repair 95 days ago. The records entry and the 'ELT not installed' placard are in place. Can you fly a for-hire trip?
options: No, the removal exception ends after 90 days
Yes, if the trip stays within 50 NM
Yes, the placard makes it legal
Yes, for up to 120 days
final_quiz.why: The removal exception requires the entry and placard and allows no operation more than 90 days after removal [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)]]. The 50 NM exception is for training only.

final_quiz.q: A flight school's ELT is inoperative. A student's dual cross-country goes to an airport 70 NM away. Does the training exception apply?
options: Yes, any training flight is exempt, because the rule excuses flight schools entirely from the ELT requirement
No, training flights never have exceptions, whatever the distance from the airport
Yes, as long as a CFI is on board and the flight is logged as dual instruction
No, it covers only training done entirely within 50 NM of the departure airport
final_quiz.why: The exception covers training operations conducted entirely within a 50 NM radius of the airport where they began [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)]].

final_quiz.q: You move from a Part 91 corporate job to a Part 135 operator. What does 91.207 require differently for the ELT?
options: Part 135 operations need an approved automatic type ELT; a personal type is not enough
Nothing changes
Part 135 airplanes need no ELT
Part 135 needs two ELTs
final_quiz.why: Part 135 operations need an approved automatic type ELT; other operations may use a personal or automatic type [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(a)]].

final_quiz.q: You are hired under Part 91 to fly a sightseer along a lake shore, never farther from shore than your power-off glide. What does 91.205(b)(12) require for this flight?
options: Life vests for the passengers only, since the flight stays near the shoreline
Approved flotation gear for each occupant and at least one pyrotechnic signaling device
A liferaft and a survival type ELT, since the flight is for hire over water
Nothing under 91.205(b)(12), since you stay within power-off gliding distance of shore
final_quiz.why: The flotation and pyrotechnic rule applies only for hire over water and beyond power-off gliding distance from shore [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(12)]]. Liferafts and a raft ELT are Part 135 extended overwater items [[6:65|14 CFR 135.167]].

final_quiz.q: In flight you see thick black smoke from the cowling. What does the AFH say this suggests, and what extra step should you consider?
options: Fuel-fed fire; open the cabin vents and keep the engine running to burn off the fuel
Oil-fed fire; consider stopping the propeller to stop the engine-driven pump feeding it
Electrical fire; turn the master off and back on to reset the circuit breakers
Carburetor ice; apply carburetor heat and expect the smoke to clear as the ice melts away
final_quiz.why: Thick black smoke points to an oil-fed fire; stopping propeller rotation stops the engine-driven pump feeding the fire [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].

final_quiz.q: An electrical fire smell develops at night in IMC, and you need the radios. What does the AFH allow, and what is the most prudent course?
options: Leave everything on and continue to destination, since the smell will clear as the wires cool down
Turn on the cabin heat to clear the smoke, then continue to an airport with better weather
Pull every circuit breaker and continue to destination using a handheld radio for navigation and a flashlight
Master off, switches off, master on, then switches on one at a time; land as soon as possible
final_quiz.why: That is the isolation sequence when power is essential, but it recreates the problem, so landing as soon as possible is most prudent [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

final_quiz.q: Ditching: the primary swell is 8 ft high, a secondary swell 3 ft high runs at right angles. Which heading?
options: Straight into the primary swell
Parallel to the primary swell and down the secondary swell
45 degrees to both, always
Directly into the wind regardless of swell
final_quiz.why: Land parallel to the primary system and down swell of the secondary; a 45 degree compromise is for equal swells [[34:50|AIM 6-3-3]].

final_quiz.q: You must ditch at night over glassy water. What does the AIM recommend for the touchdown?
options: Carry power, 9 to 12 degrees nose up, 10 to 20 percent above stall, until contact
Cut power at 50 feet above the water and let the airplane settle onto the surface
Dive to build speed and flare high to cushion the touchdown on the glassy water ahead
Land with full flaps in a low-wing airplane and cut the engine at the start of the flare
final_quiz.why: Height can be misjudged by 50 ft or more; carry enough power for 9 to 12 degrees nose up and 10 to 20 percent over stall until contact [[34:51|AIM 6-3-3]].

final_quiz.q: After an off-airport landing in remote terrain, your passengers want to hike to a road you saw 15 miles away. What does the AIM advise?
options: Hike out right away while you have energy, since a road 15 miles away is easy to reach
Split up: one stays with the airplane and one hikes toward the road to bring back help before dark
Stay with the airplane unless you believe you will not be found, and prepare to signal
Burn the airplane at once as a signal, since smoke is the surest way to be seen
final_quiz.why: Unless you have good reason to believe you won't be located, it is best to remain with the aircraft and prepare to signal search aircraft [[34:47|AIM 6-3-2]].

final_quiz.q: Before a flight in a parachute-equipped airplane, your right-seat passenger asks when she should ever pull the handle. Best answer?
options: Whenever she feels nervous about the flight, since an early deployment is always safer
Generally only if you are incapacitated; brief her on safe conditions and basic steps
Never; only the pilot may touch the handle, so she should not be briefed on it
Any time the engine runs rough, since you will not have time to troubleshoot it
final_quiz.why: Brief passengers with access on safe deployment conditions and basic steps; generally they would deploy only if the pilot were incapacitated [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

final_quiz.q: An EAL-equipped airplane is diverting after its pilot collapsed. It is 10 miles from the chosen runway at 9,000 ft MSL. What should other pilots on that CTAF expect?
options: Silence until landing
The airplane will answer traffic calls
Synthetic voice broadcasts with call sign, 'pilot incapacitation', position and time to landing, plus a one-minute-out call
It will hold until ATC clears it
final_quiz.why: Within 12 miles and at or below 12,000 ft MSL it broadcasts on tower or CTAF with those items and makes a one-minute-out call [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

final_quiz.q: Planning a winter for-hire flight into sparsely settled northern Canada, where can you learn the legal survival kit requirements?
options: 14 CFR 91.205 lists them in the equipment list for flights over remote areas
The airplane's POH, which lists the survival kit required for each region
Canadian Ministry of Transport officials (and Alaska State DOT for Alaska)
The ACS, which lists the survival gear a commercial applicant must carry
final_quiz.why: The AIM says kits are required by law for flight into sparsely settled areas of Canada and Alaska, and those officials can give the specific requirements [[34:165|AIM 7-6-9]] [[34:166|AIM 7-6-9]].

takeaways: 406 MHz ELTs get a response in minutes; 121.5 MHz units wait for someone to hear them.
ELT: inspect every 12 calendar months; battery at 1 cumulative hour or half its useful life; test only on the ground.
Extinguisher first, then ventilate; close vents if smoke grows; land as soon as possible.
Plan to last 48 to 72 hours: flight plan, water, clothing, shelter and signals you can reach.
For hire beyond gliding distance from shore: flotation for each occupant and a pyrotechnic signal.
Ditch parallel to the swell, never into its face, slow and nose up; inflate vests outside.
Brief the parachute and EAL: who, when and how, and simulate the pull, never do it.
cfi_notes: AIM paragraph numbers shift between editions. In the 2/20/25 AIM used here, ELTs are 6-2-4, 6-2-5 is the K-9 explosives program, and search and rescue (survival equipment, body signals) is 6-2-6. Cite the paragraph title, not just the number.
Examiners often ask for the ELT inspection and battery dates. Have the student find them in the logbooks and on the transmitter label before the checkride [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]].
Students mix up the 91.207 exceptions. The 50 NM exception is for training only, and the removal exception has a 90-day limit plus a placard [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)]].

Tension to discuss: the AIM says to set the radio for continuous transmission before a crash landing if fire risk is not a factor [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]], while the AFH says turning off the electrical system before touchdown reduces post-crash fire risk [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]. Both put airplane control first; teach the POH order.

The AFH ditching guidance (use no more than intermediate flaps in a low-wing, gear up) and the AIM's (best recommended speed, fully stalled as possible, or power and 10 to 20 percent above stall on glassy water) fit together; the AIM text comes from the National SAR Manual and includes multiengine advice that does not apply to ASEL [[24:356|AFH 18-7]] [[34:51|AIM 6-3-3]].

The flotation and life vest guidance in the AIM sits in the seaplane safety paragraph, but the 91.205(b)(12) rule and the 'inflate after exiting' advice apply equally to landplanes over water [[34:166|AIM 7-6-9]].
Commercial depth: have the student sort each equipment item into 'required by rule for this flight' versus 'my choice', and explain the Part 135 contrast only from the regulation text.
For S3 in parachute airplanes, rehearse the decision with scenarios (midair, control failure, incapacitation) and the arming/disarming flow; the ACS allows simulation only (ACS Appendix 3).
Some students treat survival gear as a box to check. Ask them to pack it for a real route and season and carry it on a cross-country; then ask where each item is with eyes closed.
gaps: None of these sources gives fire extinguisher types, agents, discharge times, effective range or toxic by-products for small airplanes. Use the extinguisher's label, the POH and the manufacturer's instructions.
The sources give no specific cold-weather or mountain survival kit list, no shelter guidance and no food amounts for Part 91; the 135.167 raft list is the only itemized list [[6:66|14 CFR 135.167]].

First aid for injuries is not covered beyond chemical exposure [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]] and the Part 135 kit contents for more than 19 seats [[6:72|14 CFR 135.177]]. A first aid course is CFI or outside training.
Ballistic parachute speed and altitude limits, handle forces and arming steps, and EAL activation steps, are manufacturer specific; the AFH gives only general guidance [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].
The sources do not explain how to use a pyrotechnic signal, signal mirror or dye marker; follow the device's instructions.

activities.title: True or false: ELT facts
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: A 406 MHz ELT also sends a low-power 121.5 MHz homing signal.
cards.why: True. 406 MHz ELTs include a low-power 121.5 MHz homing transmitter for the final search [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]].

cards.s: An ELT test in flight is fine if it is kept to three sweeps.
cards.why: False. Airborne tests are not authorized [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

cards.s: An activated ELT is designed to transmit for at least 48 hours.
cards.why: True. ELTs operate continuously for at least 48 hours over a wide temperature range [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]].

cards.s: A fixed automatic ELT should be mounted as far forward as practicable so it is easy to reach.
cards.why: False. Fixed and deployable automatic types go as far aft as practicable [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(b)]].

cards.s: A 406 MHz ELT must be registered with NOAA.
cards.why: True. The FCC and TSO-C126 require registration with NOAA [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]].

cards.s: An airplane equipped to carry only one person needs no ELT under 91.207.
cards.why: True. Aircraft equipped to carry not more than one person are excepted [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)]].

activities.title: What the tree landing gets right
activities.intro: Drag each description to its numbered pin.

pins.label: Wing spreading the load across the branches
Nose-high cabin, windshield kept out of the branches
Wide, dense crowns that cushion the stop
Heavy trunk the fuselage must not hit

activities.title: Who requires it?
activities.intro: Tap an item, then tap the rule (or advice) it comes from.
buckets: Any for-hire flight beyond gliding distance from shore (91.205(b)(12))

items.t: Approved flotation gear readily available to each occupant
Life preserver with a survivor locator light for each occupant
Enough liferafts for everyone on board
A survival type ELT attached to a liferaft
A survivor locator light in each liferaft
Ditch near a surface vessel if you can
A survival kit in one floatable container that is easy to reach
Take survival equipment for the climate and terrain over uninhabited land

activities.title: Put the ditching in order
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: MAYDAY on the frequency in use, or squawk 7700 if you are talking to no one
Give ELT status, color, people and equipment on board, and actuate the ELT
Look at the sea: find the primary swell and read the wind streaks
Turn to a heading parallel to the primary swell with the most headwind
Fly low over the water and slow to about ten knots above stall with power
Touch down at the lowest safe speed, nose up, on top or the back side of a swell
Get out of the airplane, then inflate the life vests

activities.title: Body signals to a rescue pilot
activities.intro: Tap a signal, then the message it sends.

pairs.l: Both arms waved across the face
pairs.r: Do not attempt to land here
Can proceed shortly, wait if practicable
Need mechanical help or parts, long delay

activities.title: Survival numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Four people may wait 72 hours after a forced landing in the desert. Using the low end of the PHAK guide (2 quarts per person per 24 hours), how many quarts of water should you carry?
items.why: 2 quarts x 4 people x 3 days = 24 quarts [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]]. The high end of the guide (4 quarts) would double it.

items.q: A new ELT battery's useful life, set by the manufacturer, is 8 years counted from 2024. Ignoring use time, in what year must it be replaced?
Your ELT went off by accident for 25 minutes last month and 40 minutes today. How many cumulative minutes has it transmitted? (Over 60 means the battery is due.)
items.why: 25 + 40 = 65 minutes, more than 1 cumulative hour, so the battery must be replaced or recharged [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]].

items.q: On a VFR flight plan your ETA at the final destination is 1415. If you never respond, at what time (hhmm) will a search start?
items.why: A search starts if you fail to respond within one-half hour after ETA: 1415 + 30 min = 1445 [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]].

items.q: Gliding at 60 knots with a 15-knot wind, you can land into the wind or downwind. How many times more crash energy does the downwind landing carry? (Energy grows with groundspeed squared.)
items.why: Groundspeeds: 60 - 15 = 45 knots and 60 + 15 = 75 knots. (75 / 45) squared = 1.667 squared = 2.78, about 2.8 times. Doubling groundspeed quadruples the energy [[24:352|AFH 18-3]].

items.q: A Part 135 liferaft rated for 6 people carries the itemized equipment list instead of a route survival kit. Planning for all 6 people, how many calories of emergency rations is the minimum?
items.why: The list calls for a 2-day supply of at least 1,000 calories per day for each person: 6 x 1,000 x 2 = 12,000 calories [[6:65|14 CFR 135.167]] [[6:66|14 CFR 135.167]].

activities.title: The photo flight over the bay
activities.intro: Your employer runs aerial photography under Part 91. Today you fly a photographer for hire in a four-seat high-wing single to shoot a lighthouse 8 NM offshore. From your planned 1,500 ft, your POH glide puts you well beyond power-off gliding distance from shore for part of the flight.

steps.s: Planning: what equipment does this flight legally need beyond the normal day VFR list?
options: Nothing extra, because a Part 91 flight needs only the standard day VFR equipment and the ELT
A liferaft with a survival-type ELT, because the route goes beyond power-off gliding distance of shore
Approved flotation gear readily available to each occupant, plus a pyrotechnic signaling device
Only a life vest for the photographer, since the pilot does not count as an occupant here
steps.why: Flying for hire over water beyond power-off gliding distance from shore requires both items [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(12)]]. Liferafts and raft ELTs are Part 135 extended overwater items [[6:65|14 CFR 135.167]].

steps.s: Preflight: the ELT's last inspection entry is 13 months old.
options: Go; the battery date is still good, and that is what the ELT rule actually checks
Go and test it in flight on 121.5 MHz to confirm that the ELT transmits before landing
Go, but stay within 50 NM of the departure airport until it can be inspected
Do not go until it is inspected; it must be inspected within 12 calendar months
steps.why: The ELT must be inspected within 12 calendar months of the last inspection [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]]. The 50 NM exception is for training only [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)]], and airborne tests are not authorized [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

steps.s: Briefing: the photographer asks what to do with the life vest if you have to ditch.
options: Wear it uninflated and inflate it only after getting out of the airplane
Inflate it now, just in case
Keep it in the bag until you are in the water
Inflate it on short final
steps.why: Approved vests are worn uninflated and inflated after exiting [[34:166|AIM 7-6-9]]. Brief their location and use before the flight [[34:166|AIM 7-6-9]].

steps.s: Offshore at 1,500 ft the engine runs rough and loses power. Shore is out of gliding range. You are not talking to anyone.
options: Stay silent and focus only on the engine until you have the airplane under control
Squawk 7700, call MAYDAY, actuate the ELT, and turn toward a boat you can see
Turn off the master to prevent a fire, then glide toward the shore you can see
Climb steeply to reach shore, trading airspeed for the extra altitude you need
steps.why: Squawk 7700 if not in contact, send a distress message, actuate the ELT, and try to ditch near a surface vessel [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]]. Use the partial power while it lasts [[34:51|AIM 6-3-3]].

steps.s: Below you, a heavy swell runs from the west. The wind is from the northwest at 15 knots.
options: Land into the wind, across the swell, even if that means touching down on a swell face
Land parallel to the swell, on the heading with more headwind, away from the swell face
Land directly into the swell face for the slowest groundspeed and the shortest touchdown run
Land downwind for a longer float, since the extra groundspeed carries you over the swells
steps.why: Avoid the face of a swell; land parallel to it and choose the parallel heading with more into-wind component, accepting crosswind [[34:50|AIM 6-3-3]].
